title: CCSDS Cryptographic Algorithms
organisation: Consultative Committee for Space Data Systems (CCSDS)
status_notes: Current issue according to the Document Control table (PDF p. 7), which lists 352.0-B-1 (October 2012) as the superseded original issue. Substantive changes from the original are marked by change bars.
summary:
The short CCSDS Recommended Standard that fixes **which cryptographic algorithms CCSDS missions use** for confidentiality, authentication and authenticated encryption. It does not say where in the stack to apply them; that is left to mission planners and to documents such as [350.0-G-3](ccsds-350-0-350x0g3.md) and the [SDLS](../ccsds/sdls.md) Blue Book ([355.0-B-2](ccsds-355-0-355x0b2.md)). Its choices are the algorithms behind SDLS baseline modes and many [CCSDS security](../ccsds/security.md) designs.

Section 2 gives the background: why civilian missions now need security, symmetric hash-based and cipher-based MACs, digital signatures and authenticated encryption (AEAD). It stresses that encryption without authentication is dangerous and highly discouraged.

The normative sections 3 and 4 make these choices:

* **Encryption**: AES for all missions, a 256-bit key for missions planned after this issue (128-bit allowed for existing implementations), and Counter Mode.
* **Authenticated encryption**: GCM with a 128-bit MAC.
* **Hash-based MAC**: HMAC (FIPS 198-1) with SHA-256 normally; SHA-224/384/512 or RIPEMD-160 by prior agreement; SHA-1 forbidden; truncation discouraged and only by agreement.
* **Cipher-based MAC**: AES-CMAC (256-bit key for new missions), with GMAC allowed when a GCM implementation is used for authentication only.
* **Digital signatures**: DSS, preferably RSA (PKCS #1 v2.1) with 4096-bit keys for new missions (2048-bit for existing), with DSA or ECDSA allowed.

Annex A discusses the threats and consequences of omitting confidentiality or authentication. It notes that all the algorithms are public domain with no known patents.

key_points.text: One symmetric encryption algorithm and one mode are recommended for all CCSDS missions; several alternative authentication/integrity algorithms are offered; how, when and where to apply them is left to mission planners.
Key management is outside the scope of the standard (see the Space Missions Key Management Concept, 350.6-G-1).
Applicable to all civilian missions needing confidentiality, authentication or authenticated confidentiality; security is encouraged especially on command links, subject to a risk analysis.
The use of encryption without authentication is highly discouraged for CCSDS missions.
All CCSDS missions shall use AES (FIPS 197, ISO/IEC 18033-3) for encryption; missions planned after issue 2 shall use 256-bit keys, while existing implementations may use 128-bit keys.
The mode of operation shall be Counter Mode; when encryption with integrity and origin authentication is needed, GCM shall be used with a 128-bit MAC.
HMAC (FIPS 198-1) with SHA (FIPS 180-4), normally SHA-256; SHA-224, SHA-384, SHA-512 or RIPEMD-160 may be used by prior agreement, and SHA-1 shall not be used.
HMAC output should not be truncated; any truncation must be agreed a priori by the communicating entities.

A cipher-based MAC shall be CMAC with AES (256-bit key for new missions; 128, 192 or 256 bits for existing ones); GMAC may replace CMAC when an authenticated-encryption implementation is used for authentication only.
Digital signatures shall follow DSS (FIPS 186-3), preferably RSA (PKCS #1 v2.1) with 4096-bit keys for new missions and 2048-bit for existing ones; DSA and ECDSA are also allowed.
Spacecraft without access to a key server can carry a pre-loaded public key cache or receive public keys by upload after launch.
If on-board security services fail and there is no bypass mode, communications may be lost entirely.
All referenced algorithms are in the public domain, and no patents are known to apply; no SANA action is required.

notes: Newer issue of the 352.0-B-1 (November 2012 in other documents; the Document Control table says October 2012) cited by ccsds-350-0-350x0g3; it is reference [10] of ccsds-350-5-350x5g2. Inconsistencies as printed: 1.1 calls [B1] 'The Application of CCSDS Protocols to Secure Systems' and 2.2 cites it as 'CCSDS 350.0-G-2', but [B1] is listed as 350.0-G-3 'The Application of Security to CCSDS Protocols' (library ccsds-350-0-350x0g3); 2.2 cites the SDLS protocol as [B7], which is the Green Book 350.5-G-1 (the library holds issue 2, ccsds-350-5-350x5g2); 4.2.2.2 cites 'RFC 6234 (reference [B20])' while [B20] is printed as RFC 4634 dated May 2011; [B8] has no RFC number; author names are duplicated in [B9] ('R. Glenn') and [B19] ('M. Bellar'). [B23] cites SDLS issue 1; the library holds issue 2 (ccsds-355-0-355x0b2). PDF pages 1 and 2 are duplicate covers; the extraction has 28 PDF pages (registry: 27), the last blank. No individual authors are named; the Secretariat e-mail address is not reproduced.
